title: Constellation Energy Generation, LLC submits Request for Clarification or, in the Alternative, Rehearing of the 12/18/2025 Order under EL25-49 et al.

documents.name: Constellation Request for Clarification.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                           BEFORE THE
                             FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.                                 )                Docket No. EL25-49-000


Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities                     )                Docket No. AD24-11-000


Constellation Energy Generation, LLC                                )
                                                                    )
      v.                                                            )                Docket No. EL25-20-000
                                                                    )                           (Consolidated)
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                         )

       REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, REHEARING
                OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC

           Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) requests clarification, or in the

alternative, rehearing, of the order issued by the Commission on December 18, 2025, in the above-

captioned dockets.1 The Commission should clarify two discrete issues. First, consistent with

existing rules for non-firm exports, a capacity resource should not be required to delist when it is

serving Co-Located Load2 taking non-firm contract demand transmission service, so long as the

capacity resource has no obligation to serve the Co-Located Load during a capacity emergency. In

that scenario, the capacity resource remains available to serve the grid when needed for resource

adequacy; forcing the capacity resource nevertheless to delist would needlessly remove available

capacity from serving the grid. Moreover, the Commission should seek to encourage this type of

arrangement—in which the generation resource remains available to the grid in capacity

emergencies, and the Co-Located Load either curtails or self-supplies using backup generation—




1
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“December 18th Order”).
2
    Unless otherwise defined, all capitalized terms have the same meaning as in the December 18th Order.
 because such an arrangement allows for the interconnection of new data center load, vital to our

national interest, without any impact on the capacity price or reliability. Second, the Commission

should clarify that it did not intend to change the scope of its jurisdiction over a generator’s

wholesale sales and transmission and, specifically, that (i) the sales and transmission between a

generator and any wholesale entity are not a “question of state law,”3 and (ii) states may not use

their jurisdiction over the allocation of the costs of interstate wholesale sales to indirectly regulate

the interconnection of generators serving Co-Located Load. To the extent that these clarifications

are denied, we respectfully seek rehearing.

                              LIST OF ERRORS/STATEMENT OF ISSUES

We seek clarification or rehearing on two issues:

          1. The Commission should clarify, that consistent with PJM’s existing tariff, capacity
             resources are not required to delist their capacity before making interruptible commitments
             to serve Co-Located Load taking non-firm contract demand transmission service, provided
             PJM can verify that the generator will be available to support the grid during capacity
             emergencies because the load is interruptible or has its own backup generation
             arrangements. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. State
             Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) (State Farm); Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y.,
             Inc. v. FERC, 45 F.4th 265 (D.C. Cir. 2022); Elec. Consumers Res. Council v. FERC, 747
             F.2d 1511, 1513-14 (D.C. Cir. 1984).

          2. The Commission should clarify that the December 18th Order did not change the scope of
             its jurisdiction over a generator’s wholesale sales and transmission. Specifically, the
             Commission should clarify that (i) sales and transmission between a generator and any
             wholesale entity are not a “question of state law”4 and (ii) that states may not use their
             jurisdiction over the allocation of the costs of interstate wholesale sales among retail
             customers to indirectly regulate the interconnection of generators serving Co-Located
             Load. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A); State Farm, 463 U.S. at 43; Elec. Consumers Res. Council
             v. FERC, 747 F.2d at 1513-14.

To the extent that the requested clarifications are denied, we respectfully request rehearing.




3
    December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 169.
4
    Id.

                                                       2
                                                   ARGUMENT

I.         The Commission Should Clarify that Capacity Resources are Not Required to Delist
           Before Making Interruptible Commitments.

           Read by its terms, the December 18th Order could appear to require the delist of capacity

resources even when the capacity resources remain fully capable of serving the grid during

capacity emergencies. The Order states, “[i]n accordance with the existing rules for removing

Capacity Resource status, … an existing generating facility may not begin serving Co-Located

Load that is not Network Load until it has delisted its [capacity interconnection rights] for the

portion of the generating facility to be designated to serve any Co-Located Load that is not

receiving [Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS)].”5

           But generators and Co-Located Load may seek contractual arrangements in which, during

a capacity emergency, the generator will serve the grid rather than the Co-Located Load. The Co-

Located Load, in turn, could either curtail or rely on its own backup generation. Constellation

seeks clarification that the Commission did not intend to discourage or frustrate those

arrangements or insist the generation that is capable of supplying the grid during a capacity

performance event delist.

           Indeed, the Commission should encourage arrangements in which Co-Located Load can

receive non-NITS service (such as non-firm contract service) and also curtail its reliance on the

Co-Located generator during capacity emergencies. Such an arrangement allows the

interconnection of new data center load, important to our economic competitiveness and national

security; the co-location of that load, minimizing the need for grid upgrades; and the continued




5
    December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 230 (citing PJM, Intra-PJM Tariffs, OATT, attach. DD.6, § 6.6 Offer
    Requirement for Capacity Resources (3.0.0); PJM March 24 Response at 58) (emphasis added).

                                                          3
 availability of the co-located generator to serve the grid when it is needed to ensure resource

adequacy. In other words, such an arrangement facilitates the prompt interconnection of new data

center load without any impact on capacity prices or reliability. Requiring the delist of capacity in

such an arrangement would needlessly reduce the capacity available for existing customers.

           It would also be inconsistent with PJM’s existing rules, which only require capacity

resources entering external sales to delist capacity interconnection rights if a resource “has a

financially and physically firm commitment to an external sale of its capacity.”6 But again, not all

agreements by Co-located Generators to serve Co-Located Load will be “physically firm

commitments.” Some may be interruptible. As the Commission recognizes, “the record

demonstrates … Co-Located Loads are willing and able to limit their energy withdrawals from the

transmission system under certain conditions.”7 Co-Located Load may likewise agree to limit their

reliance on a co-located generator under certain conditions, such as a capacity emergency, and

agree either to curtail itself or be served by backup generation or batteries.8

           Accordingly, it is vitally important for the Commission to clarify that it did not intend to

require capacity resources to delist to serve co-located loads that are taking non-firm contract

demand transmission service, so long as PJM can verify that co-located customer has no




6
    PJM Tariffs, OATT, Attachment DD.6, § 6.6 (emphasis added); see also PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. September 17,
    2007 Filing, Docket No. ER07-1050-001, at 4-5 (“[A]s set forth in the must-offer rule of section 6.6, a PJM resource
    that can qualify as a capacity resource must offer its capacity into the RPM auctions unless it can show that it is
    committed to a firm export, will be physically unavailable in the relevant delivery year, or was interconnected to the
    system as an ‘energy-only’ resource.”).
7
    December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 199; id. P 204 (“We note that, in general, special protection schemes
    allow Eligible Customers on behalf of Co-Located Load to effectively limit their withdrawals from the transmission
    system.”) (citing Constellation April 23 Reply Comments Herling Aff. ¶ 23).
8
    Constellation April 23, 2025 Reply Comments at 98 (“‘[d]ata centers almost always have their own backup power
    supply ….’”) (quoting Michael Kormos, The Co-Located Load Solution at 10; Kormos Aff., Appendix).

                                                             4
 contractual right to energy from the generator during a capacity emergency9 and has the ability to

(i) interrupt and/or (ii) turn on back-up diesels or other back-up power or draw on batteries when

transmission under the non-firm contract demand service is interrupted and the co-located

generator is serving the grid.

            To the extent there are concerns that PJM would be “in competition with non-capacity

backed co-located loads for output of a Capacity Resource,”10 the Commission could require the

Co-Located Load to disclose information regarding protective relay scheme and its interruptible

commitment, and impose penalties on that Co-Located Load for failure to comply with its

commitment.11 Those assurances could be provided by the Co-located Load confirming its

willingness and the ability to interrupt or demonstrating that it has back-up diesels or batteries that

will take over its supply. If such assurances are provided, it is not reasonable for the Commission

to require a Co-Located Generator to delist.

            Interruptible commitments are not firm. To treat them otherwise would needlessly deprive

PJM of capacity that would be committed to serve its load, compounding resource adequacy



9
    As Constellation stated in its April 23, 2025 Reply Comments, “Constellation’s view is that any Existing Generation
    Capacity Resources that would prioritize serving co-located load over following PJM dispatch should instead seek
    removal of Capacity Resource status or otherwise seek appropriate replacement capacity to cover its capacity supply
    obligation.” Constellation April 23, 2025 Reply Comments at 92-93.
10
      PJM March 24, 2025 Answer at 59; id. (“PJM cannot be simultaneously responsible for ensuring the energy needs
     of the PJM Region and unsure whether a Capacity Resource will decide to serve PJM loads or co-located loads.”)
     (emphasis in original).
11
      See December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 219 (requesting that parties answer “What are the appropriate
     rates, terms, and conditions” for new Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service
     and “What is the appropriate penalty charge or other remedial action that PJM should take to address any unreserved
     use of the PJM transmission system” for an Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand or Non-Firm Contract
     Demand). On rehearing, Indicated PJM Transmission Owners repeat their prior arguments that protective relays
     might fail. See Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, January 16, 2026 Request for Rehearing, at 39-41, 49. The
     Commission should continue to reject these arguments. As supported by Michael Kormos, the former Chief
     Operations Officer of PJM, “[p]rotective mechanisms are commonplace and frequently used by PJM and others in
     situations beyond co-located load to ensure safe and reliable grid operations, including for example, primary and
     secondary relays and redundant protection systems.” Constellation April 23, 2025 Reply Comments at 48-49 (citing
     Kormos Aff. at ¶ 6).

                                                            5
 challenges. In the event the Commission disagrees, we seek rehearing. Requiring capacity

resources to delist when arrangements other than a co-located generator are in place to curtail or

serve the large load when transmission service is interrupted would be a failure of reasoned

decision making.12 It would also be unduly discriminatory, and therefore arbitrary and capricious,

to require capacity resources serving large load to delist for entering into interruptible

commitments to serve Co-Located Load, but not requiring capacity resources to delist before

making other non-firm commitments.13

II.         The Commission Should Clarify the Scope of its Jurisdiction Over a Generator’s
            Wholesale Sales and Transmission.

            Constellation agrees with the Commission’s conclusions regarding the scope of its

jurisdiction but there are two statements in the December 18th Order that could be misinterpreted

in a manner inconsistent with settled jurisdictional principles. Accordingly, Constellation

respectfully requests that the Commission clarify the following two points.

            First, in the December 18th Order, the Commission concludes that “states have authority

over their generation resource mix, including through their siting authority” and that, therefore,

“which generating facilities are sited and allowed to serve Co-Located Load is also a question of

state law.”14 Often, however, a generator will not serve Co-Located Load directly. Rather, the




12
      See Elec. Consumers Res. Council v. FERC, 747 F.2d 1511, 1513-14 (D.C. Cir. 1984) (“We defer to the agency’s
     expertise ... so long as its decision is supported by ‘substantial evidence’ in the record and reached by ‘reasoned
     decisionmaking,’ including an examination of the relevant data and a reasoned explanation supported by a stated
     connection between the facts found and the choice made.”) (citing Burlington Truck Lines v. United States, 371 U.S.
     156, 168 (1962); Memphis Light, Gas & Water Div. v. FPC, 504 F.2d 225, 230 (D.C. Cir. 1974); 16 U.S.C. § 825l
     (1982)).
13
      5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A) (a court must set aside any Commission order that is “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of
     discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law”); see also Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y., Inc. v. FERC, 45 F.4th
     265 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (finding the Commission violated the Administrative Procedure Act for failure to provide a
     satisfactory explanation for treating projects differently).
14
     December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 169 (emphasis added).

                                                            6
 generator will first sell electricity at wholesale to an entity, such as a retail supplier, that will then

engage in the ultimate retail sale to the Co-Located Load. Such sales for resale are exclusively

within the Commission’s jurisdiction, not the states’.15 State jurisdiction is limited to the “ultimate

[retail] sale of the energy.”16 The Commission should therefore clarify that state authority does not

extend to the wholesale sale of energy by a generator to a retail supplier, even if the retail supplier

then resells that energy to a load co-located with the generator. Such jurisdiction lies exclusively

with the Commission.

            Second, in the December 18th Order, the Commission asserts that “states have exclusive

jurisdiction over how to allocate the costs of all Commission-jurisdictional rates (including for

energy, capacity, and transmission) among retail customers, including allocating costs among

different classes of retail customers.”17 While states generally do have authority over the allocation

of the costs of interstate wholesale sales among the wholesaler’s retail customers, that authority is

not unlimited. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly stated, “even when States exercise their

traditional authority over retail rates,” the “States may not seek to achieve ends, however

legitimate, through regulatory means that intrude on FERC’s authority over interstate wholesale

rates.”18




15
     See 16 U.S.C. § 824(b)(1); see also Orangeburg, S.C. v. FERC, 862 F.3d 1071, 1086-87 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (“FERC—
     not state commissions—has ‘exclusive authority to regulate the transmission and sale at wholesale of electric energy
     in interstate commerce.’”) (quoting New England Power Co. v. New Hampshire, 455 U.S. 331, 340 (1982)).
16
     New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1, 23 (2002) (emphasis removed).
17
     December 18th Order, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 167 (emphasis added).
18
      Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 164-65 (2016); see also Nantahala Power & Light Co. v.
     Thornburg, 476 U.S. 953, 966 (1986) (“Once FERC sets such a rate, a State may not conclude in setting retail rates
     that the FERC-approved wholesale rates are unreasonable.”).

                                                             7
             We therefore respectfully request that the Commission clarify that, consistent with

longstanding Supreme Court precedent,19 states do not have unlimited authority “over how to

allocate the costs of all Commission-jurisdictional rates” and that they cannot use their authority

over retail allocation to indirectly regulate the interconnection of generators serving Co-Located

Load. For instance, a state cannot impose a requirement via the exercise of their jurisdiction over

retail sales that attempts to contradict or prohibit a transaction or sale that the Commission has said

is permitted. This is not a hypothetical concern. Some utilities have in fact asked their state

commission for authority to condition retail service in the state on the load’s acceptance of a

Transmission Security Agreement that calculates its security requirement based on a gross NITS

rate despite the fact that this Commission has said that other rates must be made available.20 The

Commission should make clear that a state may not frustrate the Commission’s policy in this

manner, and, moreover, that any such Transmission Security Agreement would be unjust and

unreasonable as a matter of federal law.

                                                       CONCLUSION

            For the foregoing reasons, the Commission should clarify the December 18th Order or, in

the alternative, grant rehearing.




19
     See, e.g., Hughes, 578 U.S. at 164-65; Thornburg, 476 U.S. at 966.
20
      See Commonwealth Edison Co., Constellation Energy Generation, LLC Motion to Reopen the Evidentiary Record
     for Supplemental Discovery, Testimony, and Briefing, Illinois Commerce Comm’n Docket No. 25-0677, at 1-2
     (filed Dec. 23, 2025), https://www.icc.illinois.gov/docket/P2025-0677/documents/374492/files/656364.pdf
     (“ComEd’s proposed changes to its General Terms and Conditions referencing a requirement to enter into a
     Transmission Security Agreement (‘TSA’), and the TSA general terms and conditions shared by ComEd in this
     proceeding, assume that all customers will take Network Integration Transmission Service (‘NITS’) billed based on
     gross billing determinants, and that service will begin when network upgrades are constructed…. ComEd’s
     assumptions regarding transmission service applicable to LDPACs are no longer valid under the recent FERC
     order.”).
